# Sustainable Tourism Development Programme
## Destination Stewardship Framework — Recommendation for the Agency Board and Sponsoring Ministry

**Version 1.0 — complete. Prepared for board decision, and for prior circulation to district authorities, community and traditional-authority representatives, and the environment and antiquities agencies. Not yet for public or investor communication.**

---

### How we would ask you to use this

One note, then the substance.

This document does not propose a marketing campaign. It proposes the conditions under which a marketing campaign would be safe to run, and a sequence in which the campaign comes fourth rather than first. That ordering is the single most consequential thing in these pages, and if the board changes nothing else, we would ask it to consider changing that.

The site and locality material in §6 is offered as **working hypotheses, so that they can be corrected**. Where a district or community has its own data — or its own view of what it wants and does not want — that supersedes what we have written and the card is retired for that locality (§5.3). A card returned to us unamended will be read not as agreement but as a sign that the conversation has not yet happened, and we would come back for it.

Two courtesies before this travels further. First, that community and traditional-authority representatives see §§3, 9 and 12 and have time to respond in their own way before the ministerial pack is assembled — a programme about local authorship that arrives in a village fully formed has already contradicted itself, and people will notice that before they notice anything else. Second, that §12 (legal and consent gates) be walked through with the environment agency, the antiquities authority, the lands ministry and, where relevant, the national UNESCO commission before any part of this is described publicly. The likeliest single cause of avoidable damage is a well-intentioned announcement that reaches an investor before it reaches the people who live at the site.

---

## 1. Recommendation on a page

**Adopt a yield-and-retention strategy rather than a volume strategy: four place-and-community entitlements defined centrally as *floors*, with a formal alternative-form route where a floor cannot be met; product design, pricing, interpretation, pace and naming devolved entirely to districts and communities; a hypothecated visitor levy that makes conservation self-financing; four instrumented pilots of deliberately different design; and a published protocol binding the agency to the same discipline it asks of others.**

| | |
|---|---|
| Strategic objective | **Not more visitors. More value retained per unit of impact.** Target: visitor spend retained in-region rising from an assumed baseline of ~35% to 55%+ by Year 5, with ecological indicators stable or improving (§10) |
| Fixed nationally | **Four entitlements only** (§3) — ecological ceilings; local value capture; cultural authorship, including the right to withhold; an answered route for grievance. Each a floor, each with a named-approver alternative-form route (§3.6) |
| Devolved to districts and communities | Which visitors they seek, what is shown and what is not, pricing, interpretation, ritual, seasonality, tooling, pace, and the destination's own name. We would suggest the agency resist standardising even the name |
| Core instrument | **Hypothecated visitor levy** — bed-night and site-entry, ring-fenced by statute: 40% conservation, 35% community fund under local control, 15% infrastructure, 10% administration (§7.2) |
| Sequencing rule | **Plumbing before posters.** No international demand-generation spend in a locality until water, waste, sanitation and access capacity are verified against projected peak load (§14.1) |
| Year 1 shape | **Four pilots — one fragile ecosystem, one living-heritage settlement, one remote community-owned enterprise, one already-overloaded honeypot requiring de-load** — different in design, identical in instrumentation (§11) |
| Principal risk | Not visitor shortfall. **Elite capture and housing displacement** — value accruing to connected intermediaries, local and external, while residents absorb the costs (§13) |
| The agency's own obligation | **Published reversal protocol**: the agency may overturn a local decision, but must publish written reasons to the same audience that saw the decision, and reversal counts are reported quarterly beside destination metrics (§9.3) |
| Measurement | Retention, resident sentiment and ecological condition weighted 70%; arrival and revenue volume 30%. Volume alone never triggers a success declaration (§10) |
| Numeric failure test | International arrivals +20% or more while local retention is flat (±3pp) and resident sentiment declines = declared failure, marketing spend paused, capacity investment continues (§10.4) |
| Investment sought | **$6.8M Year 1, $14.5M Year 2** (illustrative, assumptions at §15.1), of which $2.1M is community enterprise finance and $1.3M is monitoring instrumentation — the two lines most often cut and most often fatal |
| Self-financing horizon | Levy revenue covers conservation and community fund operating cost from **Year 4**; the ask is bridging capital, not a permanent subsidy (§15.2) |
| Decisions requested | **Three** — §15.4 |
| Programme owner | Chief Executive, Tourism Agency, as sponsor; an independent Destination Stewardship Council with binding community seats constituted within 90 days of approval (§9) |

### 1.1 The core proposition, and how confident we are in it

Destinations rarely fail from too few visitors. They fail from visitors arriving faster than the capacity to absorb them and the arrangements to retain their money.

*(This is our considered assertion from practitioner experience and from comparative destination histories, not a finding derived from this region's own data — see the evidence key at §16. We flag it because the board is entitled to know which of our statements are evidenced and which are judgement.)*

The specific failure we are trying to avoid is well documented elsewhere and cheap to reproduce: a successful campaign, a three-year arrival surge concentrated on four photogenic sites, a housing market that prices out the people whose culture is the attraction, a leakage rate above 60%, and a resident population that has learned to resent the industry before the industry has learned to pay them. That outcome is worse than slow growth, because it consumes the local consent a second attempt would require. Consent, once spent, is not repurchasable at any budget.

---

## 2. Diagnosis before design

### 2.1 The framing we would gently ask the board to test

The programme is currently described as *attracting more international visitors*. The available evidence may instead describe a **value-retention and absorptive-capacity** problem wearing a marketing problem's clothing. Only one of those responds to promotion, and we would rather establish which we have before committing eight figures to the wrong one.

| Candidate constraint | What international demand-generation does to it |
|---|---|
| Genuine awareness deficit in target markets | Resolves it — this is the case where marketing is the right tool |
| Weak or absent local supply chain (food, guides, crafts, lodging) | **Amplifies harm** — demand met by imports and outside operators; leakage rises |
| Water, waste or sanitation at or near limit | **Amplifies harm** — irreversible ecological cost, and the first visible one |
| Access bottleneck (single road, single airport slot pattern) | Nothing — concentrates load rather than distributing it |
| Concentration on four sites while thirty are unvisited | Worsens — virality compounds concentration |
| Community consent not established at key sites | Worsens sharply — arrivals become an imposition, and resistance follows |
| Heritage fabric structurally fragile | **Amplifies harm** — footfall damage is cumulative and unfunded |
| Extreme seasonality producing precarious employment | Nothing — needs product design for shoulder seasons, not more shoulder-season adverts |

### 2.2 The diagnostic we propose

Twelve weeks, no design freeze and no campaign commitment until it reports:

- **Carrying-capacity assessment** at the twelve highest-pressure sites — ecological, physical, infrastructural and social thresholds, each expressed as a number with a stated confidence interval;
- **Leakage and value-chain study** — where each unit of visitor spend goes, by category, ownership and residence of owner;
- **Resident sentiment baseline** in fourteen localities, disaggregated by age, gender and livelihood, before any promotion begins, so that later movement is interpretable;
- **Consent and tenure mapping** — who holds what rights over which sites, formally and customarily, and where those two registers disagree;
- **Heritage condition survey** — structural and fabric baseline, with footfall sensitivity noted;
- **Water and waste stress test** against three projected peak-load scenarios.

Cost **$620K**. If the study finds that leakage exceeds 55% or that any of the four flagship sites is within 15% of an ecological threshold, the Year 2 promotion envelope should be redirected to supply-side development and capacity works, and the pilot scope revised before commitment. This is the cheapest consequential decision in the programme.

### 2.3 The uncomfortable question, answered rather than deferred

Will the agency be bound by the same entitlements it asks of others? If a district discovers that the agency can overturn a locally-taken decision without giving reasons — or can license a resort inside a locality that declined one — the framework becomes rhetoric and everything downstream of it is wasted. §9.3 answers this with a specific, testable, reportable mechanism, and we would ask the board to adopt or amend it rather than to note it.

---

## 3. What is fixed everywhere: four entitlements, stated as floors

Framed as what a place and its residents are entitled to, rather than as how an operator must behave, so that very different arrangements can honour them.

### 3.1 Entitlement I — ecological ceilings are numbers, and they bind
**Floor:** every designated site has a published maximum daily and peak-hour visitor number, derived from measured thresholds, reviewed annually, and enforceable against every operator including state-owned ones. Where measurement is incomplete, an interim ceiling is set at the conservative end and revised upward only on evidence — never downward under commercial pressure alone.

*The ceiling is the ceiling. A ceiling that rises whenever it is reached is not a ceiling; it is a queue-management aspiration.*

### 3.2 Entitlement II — local value capture has a floor, not an aspiration
**Floor:** in any licensed tourism operation above a defined size, (a) a minimum share of employment at supervisory level and above is held by residents of the district, on a stated glide path rather than immediately; (b) a minimum share of food, craft and service procurement is sourced within the region, verified by audit rather than by declaration; (c) concession revenue from public land and heritage sites returns a defined percentage to the locality under local control.

We would suggest glide paths with dated milestones rather than day-one quotas. A quota that cannot be met produces either non-compliance or imported "residents"; a glide path with a funded training pipeline produces the outcome the quota was reaching for.

### 3.3 Entitlement III — cultural authorship, including the right to withhold
**Floor:** the community associated with a cultural practice, site or artefact decides what is presented to visitors, in what form, at what price, and whether it is presented at all. This includes an unconditional **right to withhold** — some things are not products, and a framework that cannot say so will eventually be asked to sell them.

Practically: no ceremony scheduled for visitor convenience without the custodians' initiative; no photography where custodians have declined it; interpretation texts approved by the community before publication, in their language first; sacred and restricted sites may be closed permanently and that closure is not appealable on commercial grounds.

### 3.4 Entitlement IV — there is a route for grievance, and it is answered
**Floor:** every resident of a tourism locality has at least one accessible channel through which they can object to a tourism development, operator behaviour or agency decision **and receive a dated, substantive response**. Form is local: a village assembly, a district ombudsman, a written pre-read, a monthly market-day surgery, an SMS line. The *answered* part is the floor; the form is entirely local.

**Firewall, mandatory:** this channel is expressly **not** a corruption or safeguarding reporting channel. Objection to a development is not a protected disclosure. The two must be separately named, separately routed and separately governed, or we create legal exposure on one side and chill genuine reporting on the other (§12.4).

### 3.5 Everything else is local property
Product design, pricing, interpretation, ceremony, sequencing, symbolism, tooling, partner selection, target segments, pace, and the destination's own name.

### 3.6 The alternative-form process (in place of exemption)

We deliberately avoid the word *exemption*, and avoid asking any district to refuse. A locality that cannot meet a floor is asked instead to **propose the nearest form it can honour**, and to state what it would take to close the remainder.

| Element | Provision |
|---|---|
| Trigger | Legal impossibility, tenure conflict, or structural impossibility (not difficulty, not commercial inconvenience) |
| Form | Two pages: which floor, why, the alternative mechanism proposed, and the condition under which the floor becomes reachable |
| Approver | Chief Executive of the agency, countersigned by the district authority and the relevant sectoral regulator |
| Duration | **24 months maximum**, renewable once with fresh reasoning |
| Visibility | Entered in a publicly accessible register, reviewed quarterly by the Stewardship Council |
| Presumption | An alternative form is accepted unless materially weaker than the floor. We expect three to six across the network in Year 1 and would be suspicious of zero |
| Never available | Entitlement I ecological ceilings, and the right to withhold under III. These two do not admit alternative forms |

---

## 4. The adaptation logic

### 4.1 Four variables, rather than a general destination model

We would ask each locality to place itself on four axes only, because these four determine whether a given tourism form functions or backfires.

| Axis | The question | What it changes |
|---|---|---|
| **Fragility** | How quickly does damage become irreversible? | Whether the instrument is a cap and permit, or a price signal |
| **Livedness** | Is the site inhabited, worked and used, or is it a monument? | Whether residents can be zoned around, or must be the authors |
| **Existing load** | Is the locality below capacity, near it, or past it? | Whether the task is attraction or de-load — opposite disciplines |
| **Local enterprise depth** | Can local businesses supply what visitors need today? | Whether promotion creates income or creates imports |

### 4.2 The working rule

> Fragility and high existing load do not mean tourism is unwelcome. They mean the growth has to be **in value rather than in volume** — fewer visitors, longer stays, higher spend, deeper local sourcing, dispersed across geography and season.

The functioning equivalent of a marketing campaign, in a locality already at load, is a permit system with dynamic pricing, a second and third route that draws pressure outward, and a shoulder-season product that gives residents twelve months of work instead of four. Our practitioner judgement is that a single well-designed dispersal route moves more economic benefit than a quarter of promotional spend — offered as judgement, not as measured finding (§16), and testable inside the pilots.

### 4.3 Local leadership: a default with a visible opt-out

**Default:** locality-level programme leadership sits with people already running functioning local enterprises or already holding custodial responsibility — selected on observed practice rather than on office held.

A district wishing to depart from this default does so through a one-page note countersigned by the district authority and the programme director, logged in the same register as §3.6. Departures are expected and unremarkable; what matters is that they are visible.

Where the practitioner lead sits outside formal authority, the workable form is almost always a **pair** — the office-holder as visible patron providing cover, the practitioner as the working engine. A practitioner without a patron will in several districts be read, reasonably, as the agency not taking the district seriously.

---

## 5. Using the locality cards well

### 5.1 What they are
Starting hypotheses about context, to be returned marked up within 60 days. They describe patterns we have observed in destinations, not judgements about people.

### 5.2 What each card contains
Working hypothesis on the four axes · where the binding constraint likely sits · what to build · what to decline · failure mode · **leading indicator observable by day 90** · legal, tenure or consent watch item.

### 5.3 The supersession rule
**Where locality-level diagnostic data exists, it supersedes the card, and the card is retired for that locality.** Within-district variance routinely exceeds between-district variance; a single village's history with an earlier development frequently dominates every regional generalisation we could offer.

---

## 6. Locality typology cards

### Card A — Fragile ecosystem, low current load
| | |
|---|---|
| Hypothesis | High fragility; uninhabited or lightly inhabited; well below load; thin local enterprise base |
| Binding constraint | Absence of a ceiling *before* discovery. Once a site is popular, imposing a cap is a political act; before, it is administration |
| Build | Permit system with dynamic pricing and advance ballot; mandatory accredited local guiding; hardened trails and viewing infrastructure ahead of demand; a research and monitoring station co-located with the visitor function |
| Decline | Road upgrades that reduce journey time below the friction the ecosystem depends on; any accommodation inside the boundary; cruise or coach access without a berth/slot cap |
| Failure mode | Single viral image, arrivals treble in eighteen months, ceiling set retrospectively
